q: The human heart is enclosed in a double-walled protective sac called the:
x: The pericardium is the double-walled sac around the heart. The pleura covers the lungs, the peritoneum lines the abdominal cavity and the meninges cover the brain and spinal cord.

q: The main function of the pericardial fluid is to:
o: Supply oxygen to the heart muscle
Reduce friction as the heart beats
Conduct the impulse from the SA node
x: Pericardial fluid lies between the two layers of the pericardium and lubricates them, so the beating heart moves with little friction. The heart muscle gets its oxygen from the coronary arteries.

q: The thick middle layer of the heart wall, made of cardiac muscle, is the:
x: The heart wall has three layers: the outer epicardium, the thick muscular myocardium and the inner endocardium. Contraction of the myocardium pumps the blood.

q: The smooth inner lining of the heart chambers, continuous with the lining of the blood vessels, is the:
x: The endocardium is a thin endothelial layer lining the chambers and covering the valves; it is continuous with the endothelium of the vessels. The epicardium is the outer layer of the heart wall.

q: Which chamber of the human heart has the thickest muscular wall?
x: The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps blood into the aorta and around the whole body. Atria have thin walls as they only push blood into the ventricles.

q: The wall of the left ventricle is thicker than that of the right ventricle because the left ventricle:
o: Contains the pacemaker tissue of the heart
Must pump blood at higher pressure through the whole systemic circuit
Pumps a much larger volume of blood per beat than the right ventricle
Pumps deoxygenated blood, which needs more force
x: The left ventricle drives blood through the long, high-resistance systemic circuit, so it needs more muscle. Both ventricles pump the same volume per beat; the right one only pumps to the nearby lungs.

q: The right atrium of the human heart receives:
o: Oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins
Deoxygenated blood from the pulmonary arteries
Deoxygenated blood from the superior and inferior venae cavae
x: The superior and inferior venae cavae return deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium. Pulmonary veins bring oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

q: The left atrium of the human heart receives:
o: Deoxygenated blood from the venae cavae
Oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins
Deoxygenated blood from the pulmonary arteries
x: Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs into the left atrium. The venae cavae open into the right atrium, and the pulmonary arteries carry blood away from the heart to the lungs.

q: The valve between the right atrium and the right ventricle is the:
x: The right atrioventricular valve has three cusps and is called the tricuspid valve. The bicuspid valve guards the left atrioventricular opening.

q: The bicuspid valve, which guards the opening between the left atrium and left ventricle, is also called the:
x: The bicuspid valve has two cusps and is also known as the mitral valve. The aortic and pulmonary valves are semilunar valves at the exits of the ventricles.

q: The chordae tendineae attached to the atrioventricular valves:
o: Carry the impulse from the AV node to the ventricles
Open the semilunar valves at the start of ventricular systole
Attach the heart to the inner layer of the pericardium
Stop the valve cusps from turning back into the atria when the ventricles contract
x: The chordae tendineae are tough cords that hold the cusps of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves, so high ventricular pressure cannot push them inside out into the atria. Impulses are carried by the bundle of His and Purkinje fibres, not by these cords.

q: In the ventricles, the chordae tendineae are anchored to small muscular projections of the wall called:
x: Chordae tendineae run from the valve cusps to papillary muscles on the ventricular wall. Purkinje fibres and bundle branches are conducting tissue, not anchors for the valves.

q: Semilunar valves are found:
o: In the wall between the two atria
Between the atria and the ventricles
At the bases of the aorta and the pulmonary trunk
At the openings of the venae cavae
x: There are two semilunar valves: the aortic valve where the aorta leaves the left ventricle and the pulmonary valve where the pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle. The valves between atria and ventricles are the tricuspid and bicuspid valves.

q: Blood pumped out of the right ventricle enters the:
x: The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary trunk, which divides into pulmonary arteries going to the lungs. The aorta leaves the left ventricle.

q: Which blood vessel carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart?
x: The pulmonary artery takes deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. It is an artery because it carries blood away from the heart, not because of its oxygen content. The aorta and coronary arteries carry oxygenated blood.

q: Which is the correct path of blood from the right atrium to the aorta?
o: Right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary veins, left atrium, left ventricle
Right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary veins, left ventricle, left atrium
Right ventricle, pulmonary veins, lungs, pulmonary artery, left atrium, left ventricle
Left atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary veins, left ventricle
x: From the right atrium blood passes through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle, then the pulmonary artery to the lungs. It returns by pulmonary veins to the left atrium, passes the bicuspid valve to the left ventricle, and leaves through the aorta.

q: The muscle of the heart wall itself receives its blood supply from the:
o: Blood in its chambers, by direct diffusion
Coronary arteries, which branch from the aorta
x: The thick heart wall cannot be supplied by diffusion from blood in the chambers, so it has its own coronary arteries arising from the base of the aorta. Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

q: The left and right ventricles are separated from each other by the:
x: A thick muscular wall, the interventricular septum, divides the two ventricles so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix. The interatrial septum separates the two atria.

q: The pacemaker of the human heart is the:
x: The sinoatrial (SA) node starts each heartbeat and sets its rhythm, so it is called the pacemaker. The AV node, bundle of His and Purkinje fibres pass the impulse on.

q: The SA node is located in the:
o: Wall of the left ventricle near the apex
Wall of the left atrium near the pulmonary veins
Wall of the right atrium near the opening of the superior vena cava
x: The SA node is a small mass of specialised cardiac muscle in the upper wall of the right atrium, close to where the superior vena cava enters. The bundle of His, not the SA node, runs in the interventricular septum.

q: The bundle of His carries the cardiac impulse down the interventricular septum from the:
x: The AV node passes the impulse into the bundle of His, which divides into right and left branches in the septum and ends in Purkinje fibres. The SA node first excites the atria, which then excite the AV node.

q: The function of the Purkinje fibres is to:
o: Delay the impulse between the atria and the ventricles
Spread the impulse quickly through the ventricle walls so they contract together
Generate the impulse that starts each heartbeat
Carry oxygenated blood to the cardiac muscle
x: Purkinje fibres conduct impulses rapidly through the ventricular walls so the ventricles contract as a unit. The SA node starts the beat and the AV node causes the delay.

q: Which is the correct order in which the cardiac impulse travels?
o: AV node, SA node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres
SA node, AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres
SA node, bundle of His, AV node, Purkinje fibres
SA node, AV node, Purkinje fibres, bundle of His
x: The impulse starts at the SA node, spreads over the atria to the AV node, then passes down the bundle of His and its branches, and finally through the Purkinje fibres in the ventricle walls.

q: The human heart is called myogenic because:
o: It is made only of smooth muscle
It beats only when stimulated by nerves from the brain
Its beat starts in specialised cardiac muscle within the heart itself
Its muscle is under voluntary control
x: In a myogenic heart the impulse arises in the heart muscle itself, at the SA node, so the heart keeps beating even without nerve supply. Nerves only speed up or slow down the rate.

q: Increased impulses through the vagus nerve to the heart cause the:
o: SA node to stop forming its own impulses permanently
x: The vagus (parasympathetic) nerve slows the SA node and so lowers the heart rate. Sympathetic nerves and adrenaline speed it up. The heart's own rhythm continues; nerves only change its rate.

q: The human heart lies in the:
o: Abdominal cavity just below the diaphragm
Right side of the chest, outside the rib cage
Thoracic cavity between the two lungs, tilted to the left
x: The heart lies in the chest (thoracic) cavity between the lungs, above the diaphragm and behind the sternum, with its apex pointing to the left.

q: A newborn has a hole in the interventricular septum. Which result is expected?
o: Some oxygenated blood passes from the left ventricle into the right ventricle
The SA node cannot produce impulses
Blood leaks from the aorta back into the left ventricle
Deoxygenated blood passes from the right atrium into the left atrium
x: The left ventricle develops higher pressure than the right, so blood is pushed through the septal hole from left to right, mixing oxygenated blood into the right side. A hole between the atria would involve the atria, and aortic backflow is a valve fault.

q: Which statement about the atria is correct?
o: The left atrium has a thicker wall than the left ventricle
Their walls are thinner than those of the ventricles because they only push blood into the ventricles
They pump blood directly to the lungs and the body
Semilunar valves guard the openings from the atria into the ventricles
x: Atria only need to push blood a short distance into the ventricles, so their walls are thin. The ventricles pump blood out of the heart, and atrioventricular (not semilunar) valves separate atria from ventricles.

q: How many pulmonary veins open into the left atrium of the human heart?
x: Four pulmonary veins, two from each lung, bring oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

q: Veins draining the heart muscle return their blood mainly into the:
x: The coronary veins collect deoxygenated blood from the heart wall and empty, through the coronary sinus, into the right atrium, like the rest of the body's deoxygenated blood.

q: Which statement about the human heart is NOT correct?
o: Valves keep blood flowing in one direction through the heart
The right side of the heart pumps oxygenated blood to the body
The heartbeat starts in the heart muscle itself
The heart has two atria and two ventricles
x: The right side of the heart handles deoxygenated blood and pumps it to the lungs; the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body. The other statements are correct.

q: Human circulation is called double circulation because:
o: Blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit of the body
Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix in the ventricles
The heart has two separate pacemakers
Blood passes through the lungs twice in one circuit
x: In one full circuit blood goes through the heart once on the pulmonary route (heart to lungs to heart) and once on the systemic route (heart to body to heart). The two kinds of blood are kept separate.

q: At a heart rate of 75 beats per minute, one complete cardiac cycle lasts about:
x: Sixty seconds divided by 75 beats gives 0.8 second for each cardiac cycle.

q: At a heart rate of 75 beats per minute, ventricular systole lasts about:
x: Ventricular systole takes about 0.3 second of the 0.8-second cycle. About 0.4 second is complete diastole, when all chambers are relaxed, and 0.8 second is the whole cycle.

q: At 75 beats per minute, the phase in which all four chambers are relaxed (complete cardiac diastole) lasts about:
x: In a 0.8-second cycle, complete diastole lasts about 0.4 second, during which blood flows from the veins into the atria and on into the ventricles. Ventricular systole lasts about 0.3 second.

q: At 75 beats per minute, ventricular systole lasts 0.3 second. For how long in each cycle are the ventricles relaxed?
x: The whole cycle is 0.8 second, so the ventricles are relaxed for 0.8 minus 0.3 = 0.5 second. This includes complete diastole and the time of atrial systole, when the ventricles are still relaxed.

q: The contraction phase of a chamber of the heart is called:
x: Systole is contraction of a heart chamber and diastole is its relaxation. Fibrillation is uncoordinated twitching of heart muscle.

q: During ventricular systole, the condition of the heart valves is:
o: Atrioventricular valves open, semilunar valves open
Atrioventricular valves closed, semilunar valves open
Atrioventricular valves open, semilunar valves closed
x: When the ventricles contract, their rising pressure shuts the tricuspid and bicuspid valves and forces the semilunar valves open, so blood leaves through the aorta and pulmonary trunk.

q: During complete cardiac diastole:
o: Semilunar valves are open and blood flows from the arteries into the ventricles
All valves are closed and no blood enters the heart
Atrioventricular valves are open and blood flows passively from the atria into the ventricles
The ventricles contract and push blood into the atria
x: With all chambers relaxed, the semilunar valves are shut and the atrioventricular valves are open, so blood returning from the veins flows through the atria into the ventricles.

q: The first heart sound, 'lubb', is produced by the:
o: Opening of the atrioventricular valves during diastole
Closure of the atrioventricular valves at the start of ventricular systole
Closure of the semilunar valves at the start of ventricular diastole
x: 'Lubb' is caused by the tricuspid and bicuspid valves snapping shut as the ventricles begin to contract. 'Dubb', the second sound, comes from closure of the semilunar valves.

q: The second heart sound, 'dubb', is produced by the:
o: Rush of blood into the atria from the veins
Closure of the atrioventricular valves at the beginning of ventricular systole
Closure of the semilunar valves at the beginning of ventricular diastole
Opening of the semilunar valves during ventricular systole
x: When the ventricles relax, blood in the aorta and pulmonary trunk tends to flow back and shuts the semilunar valves, giving the 'dubb' sound. 'Lubb' comes from closing atrioventricular valves.

q: If the bicuspid valve does not close completely, during ventricular systole some blood will leak from the:
o: Left atrium into the left ventricle
Right ventricle into the right atrium
Left ventricle into the left atrium
x: The bicuspid valve should close when the left ventricle contracts. If it leaks, high ventricular pressure pushes some blood backward into the left atrium. Backflow from the aorta would be a fault of the aortic semilunar valve.

q: A doctor listens to the heart sounds with a:
x: A stethoscope is used to hear the 'lubb' and 'dubb' sounds. A sphygmomanometer measures blood pressure and an electrocardiograph records the heart's electrical activity.

q: An electrocardiogram (ECG) is a record of the heart's:
x: An ECG records the electrical changes (depolarisation and repolarisation) that spread through the heart during each beat, picked up by electrodes on the skin.

q: In a normal ECG, the P wave represents:
x: The P wave is the spread of the impulse from the SA node over the atria (atrial depolarisation), which is followed by atrial contraction. The QRS complex and T wave belong to the ventricles.

q: In a normal ECG, the QRS complex represents:
o: Repolarisation of the SA node only
x: The QRS complex is the rapid spread of the impulse through the ventricles (ventricular depolarisation), just before they contract. The P wave is atrial depolarisation.

q: In a normal ECG, the T wave represents:
o: Delay of the impulse at the AV node
x: The T wave shows the ventricles recovering (repolarising) after contraction. Ventricular depolarisation is the QRS complex.

q: Atrial repolarisation does not appear as a separate wave in a normal ECG because it:
o: Is recorded as the T wave
Does not occur, since atria never repolarise
Happens at the same time as the larger QRS complex and is hidden by it
Happens before the P wave of the same beat
x: The atria repolarise while the ventricles are depolarising, so the small atrial signal is masked by the much larger QRS complex. The T wave is ventricular repolarisation.

q: The short delay of the impulse at the AV node is important because it:
o: Lets the ventricles contract before the atria
Lets the atria finish contracting and fill the ventricles before the ventricles contract
Allows the SA node to rest between beats
Allows the semilunar valves to close before atrial systole
x: The AV node holds the impulse briefly, so atrial systole is complete and the ventricles are full before ventricular systole begins.

q: Which is the correct order of the phases of one heartbeat?
o: Complete diastole, ventricular systole, atrial systole
Ventricular systole, atrial systole, complete diastole
Atrial systole, ventricular systole, complete diastole
Atrial systole, complete diastole, ventricular systole
x: Each beat begins with the atria contracting, then the ventricles contract, and then all chambers relax (complete diastole) and refill before the next atrial systole.

q: Which statement about atrial systole is correct?
o: The semilunar valves open to let blood enter the ventricles
The ventricles contract at the same moment as the atria
The atria contract and push blood into the aorta and pulmonary trunk
The atria contract and push the remaining blood into the ventricles through open atrioventricular valves
x: In atrial systole both atria contract and top up the relaxed ventricles through the open tricuspid and bicuspid valves. Blood enters the arteries only during ventricular systole.

q: Most of the filling of the ventricles with blood takes place:
o: Only while the semilunar valves are open
Passively during diastole, before the atria contract
x: During diastole blood flows from the veins through the atria into the relaxed ventricles; most ventricular filling happens this way. Atrial systole then adds the remaining smaller part.

q: Cardiac output is the:
o: Volume of blood pumped by one ventricle in a single beat
Volume of blood pumped by one ventricle per minute
Pressure of blood in the aorta during systole
x: Cardiac output is the volume each ventricle pumps per minute; it equals stroke volume (volume per beat) multiplied by heart rate.

q: A person's stroke volume is 70 mL and heart rate is 75 beats per minute. The cardiac output is about:
x: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 70 mL × 75 = 5250 mL, which is about 5.25 litres per minute.

q: After the SA node fires, which part of the heart contracts first?
x: The impulse from the SA node spreads over the walls of both atria, so the two atria contract together (atrial systole) before the impulse reaches the ventricles through the AV node.

q: The Purkinje fibres carry the impulse first to the apex, so ventricular contraction starts at the apex and moves upward. This helps to:
o: Push blood back into the atria
Squeeze blood up into the aorta and pulmonary trunk
x: The arteries leave from the top (base) of the ventricles, so contraction moving from the apex upward pushes blood towards these exits, like squeezing a tube from its closed end.

q: The aortic semilunar valve opens when:
o: Pressure in the aorta rises above pressure in the left ventricle
Pressure in the left ventricle rises above pressure in the aorta
x: Valves open and close because of pressure differences. As the left ventricle contracts its pressure rises, and when it exceeds aortic pressure the semilunar valve is pushed open.

q: There is a short period in the cardiac cycle when all four heart valves are closed. Among these, it occurs:
o: In the middle of ventricular systole while blood is being ejected
At the start of ventricular systole, before ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure
While the ventricles are filling passively in diastole
x: At the start of ventricular systole the atrioventricular valves have just closed, but the semilunar valves are not yet open, so for a moment all four are shut. During atrial systole and passive filling the atrioventricular valves are open; during ejection the semilunar valves are open.

q: The normal resting heart rate of a healthy adult is about:
x: A healthy adult heart beats about 70 to 75 times per minute at rest; the textbook cardiac cycle is worked out for 75 beats per minute.

q: During exercise the heart rate rises mainly because of:
o: Sympathetic nerve impulses and the hormone adrenaline
More impulses through the vagus nerve
x: Sympathetic nerves and adrenaline make the SA node fire faster, raising the heart rate. Vagus nerve impulses do the opposite and slow the heart.

q: The impulse from the atria can reach the ventricles only through the AV node and bundle of His because:
o: The SA node lies in the ventricles
The atrioventricular valves conduct the impulse
The ventricles have no cardiac muscle
Non-conducting fibrous tissue separates the atrial muscle from the ventricular muscle
x: A ring of fibrous connective tissue between atria and ventricles does not conduct impulses, so the only path is through the AV node and bundle of His. This allows the delay that lets the atria empty first.

q: In an ECG, the QRS complex is immediately followed by:
o: Spread of the impulse from the SA node
x: The QRS complex is ventricular depolarisation, which triggers ventricular systole. Atrial contraction follows the P wave, and ventricular relaxation follows the T wave.

q: During ventricular systole, the left ventricle pumps blood into the:
x: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta, which carries it to the body. The right ventricle pumps into the pulmonary trunk.

q: Which statement about the cardiac cycle at 75 beats per minute is correct?
o: Ventricular systole lasts longer than complete diastole
Both heart sounds are produced during atrial systole
The atria and the ventricles never contract at the same moment
Atrial systole lasts longer than ventricular systole
x: Atrial systole comes first and ventricular systole follows, so the two never contract together. Ventricular systole (0.3 s) is shorter than complete diastole (0.4 s), atrial systole is the shortest phase, and both heart sounds are linked to ventricular events.

q: Blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart are called:
x: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry it back towards the heart. Venules are small veins.

q: The smallest blood vessels, through whose walls materials are exchanged with the tissues, are the:
x: Capillaries are the tiniest vessels and have walls only one cell thick, so oxygen, nutrients and wastes pass between blood and tissue fluid through them.

q: The wall of a blood capillary consists of:
o: Three layers: endothelium, smooth muscle and connective tissue
A thick layer of collagen fibres
A single layer of endothelial cells
Smooth muscle and elastic fibres only
x: A capillary wall is just endothelium, one cell thick, on a basement membrane. This thinness allows rapid diffusion. Arteries and veins have three-layered walls.

q: The middle layer (tunica media) of the wall of arteries and veins is made mainly of:
x: The tunica media contains smooth muscle and elastic fibres. It is much thicker in arteries than in veins. The inner layer is endothelium and the outer layer is connective tissue.

q: The outermost layer (tunica externa) of arteries and veins consists mainly of:
o: Connective tissue rich in collagen fibres
x: The tunica externa is tough connective tissue, mainly collagen, that protects the vessel and anchors it to surrounding tissues.

q: Compared with an artery of about the same size, a vein has:
o: A thinner wall and a larger lumen
A thicker wall and a narrower lumen
x: Veins carry blood at low pressure, so their walls (especially the muscular media) are thinner and their lumen is wider. Arteries have thick muscular, elastic walls and a narrower lumen.

q: Valves that keep blood flowing in one direction are found along the length of:
o: Veins, especially those of the limbs
x: Veins, particularly in the arms and legs, have pocket-like valves. Arteries do not need them because the high pressure from the heart keeps blood moving forward; capillaries and arterioles have no valves.

q: The function of the valves in veins is to:
o: Prevent backflow of blood and keep it moving towards the heart
Raise blood pressure in the veins
Allow exchange of gases with tissues
x: Venous valves close if blood starts to flow backward, so blood can move only towards the heart. They do not pump; the squeezing of nearby muscles pushes the blood.

q: Blood in the leg veins returns to the heart against gravity mainly because:
o: The left ventricle produces high pressure in the veins
Contracting skeletal muscles squeeze the veins and valves prevent backflow
The thick muscular wall of the veins contracts strongly
Capillaries pump blood into the veins
x: Venous pressure is low, so return from the legs depends mainly on the skeletal muscle pump: contracting leg muscles squeeze the veins, and the valves allow flow only towards the heart. Veins have thin walls with little muscle.

q: Elastic fibres in the walls of large arteries such as the aorta allow them to:
o: Exchange gases with the surrounding tissues
Prevent backflow of blood by forming valves
Stretch during ventricular systole and recoil during diastole, keeping blood moving
Store large volumes of blood at low pressure
x: Large arteries stretch as blood is pumped in and then recoil, pushing blood onward even while the ventricles relax. This smooths the flow. Veins, not arteries, act as low-pressure reservoirs.

q: The pulse felt at the wrist is due to:
o: Expansion and recoil of the artery wall with each ventricular contraction
Flow of lymph through lymph vessels
Contraction of the muscles in the walls of veins
x: Each ventricular systole sends a surge of blood that stretches the arteries; the stretch and recoil travel along the artery wall and can be felt as the pulse over an artery such as the radial artery at the wrist.

q: Arterioles control the amount of blood reaching a tissue by:
o: Contraction or relaxation of the smooth muscle in their walls
Changing the thickness of their endothelium
x: Smooth muscle in arteriole walls contracts (vasoconstriction) to narrow them and relaxes (vasodilation) to widen them, so the blood supply to each tissue can be adjusted. Arterioles have no valves.

q: Blood leaving a capillary bed first enters the:
x: Capillaries join to form venules, which unite to form veins. Arterioles bring blood into the capillary bed.

q: In the systemic circulation, blood pressure is:
o: Highest in the veins and lowest in the arteries
Highest in the aorta and lowest in the venae cavae
The same in all blood vessels
Highest in the capillaries and lowest in the aorta
x: Pressure is greatest where the left ventricle pumps blood into the aorta and falls steadily through arteries, arterioles and capillaries, so it is lowest in the large veins entering the right atrium.

q: Blood flows most slowly in the capillaries mainly because:
o: Each capillary has a thick muscular wall
Capillaries have valves that slow the flow
The total cross-sectional area of all the capillaries is very large
Capillaries lie farther from the heart than the veins do
x: Although each capillary is tiny, there are so many that their combined cross-sectional area is far greater than that of the aorta, so blood slows down there. The slow flow gives time for exchange.

q: Which of the following is NOT a reason why capillaries are well suited to exchange materials?
o: Together they give a very large surface area
Their walls contain a thick layer of smooth muscle
Their walls are only one cell thick
x: Capillary walls have no smooth muscle; they are only endothelium. Thin walls, slow flow and a huge total surface area are what make exchange efficient.

q: At the arterial end of a capillary, fluid moves out into the tissue spaces because:
o: Blood pressure there is greater than the osmotic pressure of the plasma proteins
Tissue fluid pressure is higher than blood pressure
Osmotic pressure of the plasma proteins is greater than blood pressure
The capillary wall actively pumps water out
x: At the arterial end the hydrostatic (blood) pressure is higher than the osmotic pull of plasma proteins, so water and small solutes are forced out. At the venous end blood pressure has fallen and osmotic pressure draws fluid back in.

q: The normal blood pressure of a healthy young adult is about:
x: Normal adult blood pressure is about 120/80 mmHg: 120 is the systolic and 80 the diastolic pressure. Systolic is always the higher value.

q: In a blood pressure reading of 120/80 mmHg, the value 120 is the pressure in the arteries during:
x: The upper (systolic) value is the peak arterial pressure while the ventricles contract. The lower (diastolic) value is the arterial pressure while the ventricles relax.

q: Blood pressure is measured with an instrument called a:
x: A sphygmomanometer (with an inflatable cuff) measures arterial blood pressure. A stethoscope is often used with it to listen, but it does not measure pressure by itself.

q: The hepatic portal vein is unusual because it:
o: Carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart
Carries blood from the capillaries of the gut to capillaries in the liver
Carries blood directly from the left ventricle to the liver
Has the thickest muscular wall of any vessel
x: A portal vein begins in one capillary bed and ends in another. The hepatic portal vein brings blood rich in absorbed food from the gut capillaries to the liver before it returns to the heart.

q: Which statement about arteries is correct?
o: All arteries carry blood away from the heart, but not all carry oxygenated blood
Arteries have thinner walls than veins of the same size
Arteries have valves along their length
x: Arteries are defined by direction: they carry blood away from the heart. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood. Arteries have thick walls and no valves along their length.

q: A microscope slide shows a vessel with a thick muscular and elastic wall, a narrow round lumen and no valves. The vessel is:
x: A thick tunica media with much smooth muscle and elastic tissue, a narrow round lumen and no valves are features of an artery. Veins have thin walls, wide often collapsed lumens and valves; capillaries have only endothelium.

q: At rest, which vessels hold the largest share of the body's blood and act as blood reservoirs?
x: Thin-walled, easily stretched veins hold most of the blood volume at rest, so they act as reservoirs. Arteries hold less blood but at higher pressure.

q: Rings of smooth muscle called precapillary sphincters control:
o: The return of blood in the leg veins
The movement of lymph into lymph nodes
The flow of blood into individual capillary beds
The closure of the heart valves
x: Precapillary sphincters at the entrance of capillaries contract to shut off a capillary bed or relax to open it, adjusting supply to the needs of the tissue.

q: Capillaries have no smooth muscle in their walls. Because of this, capillaries cannot:
x: Without a muscular layer a capillary cannot constrict or dilate by itself; that control is by arterioles and precapillary sphincters. Diffusion and exchange need only the thin endothelial wall.

q: The internal diameter of a blood capillary is roughly:
o: 8 to 10 micrometres, about the width of a red blood cell
x: Capillaries are so narrow that red blood cells pass through almost in single file. About 2.5 cm is the width of the aorta.

q: The largest artery of the human body is the:
x: The aorta leaves the left ventricle and is the largest artery; all systemic arteries branch from it.

q: Blood comes out of a cut blood vessel in spurts that match the heartbeat. The vessel that has been cut is:
x: Arteries carry blood at high, pulsating pressure, so a cut artery spurts in time with each ventricular contraction. Blood from a cut vein flows out steadily at low pressure.

q: Which comparison of arteries and veins is correct?
o: Arteries: thick tunica media, no valves, high pressure. Veins: thin tunica media, valves, low pressure
Arteries: thin tunica media, valves, low pressure. Veins: thick tunica media, no valves, high pressure
Arteries: thick tunica media, valves, low pressure. Veins: thin tunica media, no valves, high pressure
Arteries: thin tunica media, no valves, high pressure. Veins: thick tunica media, valves, low pressure
x: Arteries need thick muscular, elastic walls to withstand high pulsating pressure and have no valves. Veins carry blood at low pressure, have thinner walls and use valves to stop backflow.

q: The innermost layer of a blood vessel, which is in direct contact with the blood, is made of:
x: The tunica intima is a smooth lining of flat endothelial cells, giving little friction to flowing blood. Smooth muscle is in the middle layer and collagen in the outer layer.

q: Lymph is formed from:
o: Tissue fluid that enters lymph capillaries
x: Tissue (interstitial) fluid that is not returned to the blood capillaries drains into lymph capillaries; once inside them it is called lymph.

q: Lymph capillaries differ from blood capillaries in that they:
o: Are open at both ends and less permeable
Are closed at one end and are more permeable
x: Lymph capillaries begin blindly in the tissues and are more permeable than blood capillaries, so they can take up tissue fluid, proteins and even bacteria. They carry no red blood cells.

q: Compared with blood plasma, lymph:
o: Has more protein and many red blood cells
Has less protein, no red blood cells and many lymphocytes
Contains platelets and red blood cells but no lymphocytes
x: Lymph comes from tissue fluid, which has fewer proteins than plasma because large proteins mostly stay in blood. It has no red blood cells but carries many lymphocytes, especially after passing through lymph nodes.

q: The largest lymph vessel of the body is the:
x: The thoracic duct is the main and largest lymph vessel; it collects lymph from most of the body. The inferior vena cava is a vein, not a lymph vessel.

q: The thoracic duct empties lymph into the:
x: The thoracic duct runs up through the thorax and opens into the left subclavian vein near its junction with the left internal jugular vein. The right lymphatic duct opens into the right subclavian vein.

q: The right lymphatic duct drains lymph from the:
o: Left arm and left side of the head
Right side of the head and neck, right arm and right side of the thorax
Whole lower half of the body
x: The right lymphatic duct collects lymph only from the right upper part of the body. The thoracic duct drains everything else, including both legs and the intestines.

q: Lymph from the right leg returns to the blood through the:
o: Hepatic portal vein into the liver
Thoracic duct into the left subclavian vein
Inferior vena cava directly, without a duct
Right lymphatic duct into the right subclavian vein
x: The thoracic duct drains the whole lower body, both legs included, and empties into the left subclavian vein. The right lymphatic duct drains only the right upper quarter of the body, so being on the right side is not enough.

q: Lymph moves through the lymph vessels mainly because of:
o: Squeezing by skeletal muscles and breathing movements, with valves preventing backflow
Pumping by the heart, which is connected directly to the lymph vessels
x: The lymphatic system has no pump. Contraction of skeletal muscles, pressure changes during breathing and some smooth muscle in vessel walls push lymph along, and valves keep it moving one way.

q: Which statement about lymph vessels is correct?
o: Like veins, they have valves that keep lymph flowing in one direction
They carry lymph away from the heart to the tissues
They carry oxygenated blood to the lymph nodes
They have walls thicker than those of arteries
x: Lymph vessels resemble thin-walled veins and contain many valves, so lymph flows only towards the large ducts and the veins near the heart.

q: The lymph capillaries in the villi of the small intestine, which absorb fats, are called:
x: Each villus contains a lymph capillary called a lacteal, which absorbs digested fats and carries them into the lymphatic system.

q: After a fatty meal, lymph draining from the small intestine looks milky. This milky lymph is called:
x: Fat droplets absorbed by the lacteals make the lymph milky; this fat-rich lymph is chyle. Chyme is the partly digested food leaving the stomach.

q: The main function of lymph nodes is to:
o: Produce red blood cells in adults
Absorb digested fat from the intestine
Filter lymph and destroy pathogens using lymphocytes and macrophages
x: Lymph nodes are placed along lymph vessels and act as filters. Macrophages engulf bacteria and debris, and lymphocytes start immune responses. They do not pump lymph.

q: During a throat infection, the lymph nodes in the neck often become swollen and tender because:
o: Their valves are blocked by fat
Lymphocytes in them multiply to fight the infection
They are filled with red blood cells
x: Pathogens carried in lymph from the throat are trapped in nearby neck nodes, where lymphocytes multiply to fight them, so the nodes enlarge and become tender.

q: Clusters of lymph nodes are found especially in the:
x: Lymph nodes occur in groups along lymph vessels, especially in the neck (cervical), armpits (axillary) and groin (inguinal).

q: In the human body, the spleen is located in the:
o: Upper left side of the abdominal cavity, below the diaphragm
Lower right side of the abdomen, near the appendix
Neck, on either side of the windpipe
x: The spleen is the largest lymphoid organ and lies in the upper left part of the abdomen, just below the diaphragm. The thymus lies behind the sternum.

q: The spleen is sometimes called the 'graveyard of red blood cells' because it:
o: Converts red blood cells into lymphocytes
Produces all red blood cells in adults
Removes and destroys old, worn-out red blood cells
x: Macrophages in the spleen break down aged red blood cells and recycle their iron. In adults red blood cells are made in red bone marrow, not in the spleen.

q: Which of the following is NOT a function of the spleen?
x: Bile is made by the liver. The spleen breaks down old red cells, stores some blood and contains lymphocytes and macrophages that defend against blood-borne pathogens.

q: The thymus gland is located in the:
o: Thorax, behind the sternum and above the heart
x: The thymus is a lymphoid organ in the upper chest, behind the breastbone and in front of the upper part of the heart.

q: The main role of the thymus in the lymphatic system is the:
o: Destruction of old red blood cells
x: Immature lymphocytes from the bone marrow travel to the thymus, where they mature into T-lymphocytes (the T stands for thymus). The spleen destroys old red blood cells.

q: Which statement about the thymus is correct?
o: It is large and active in childhood and becomes smaller after puberty
It is found in the abdomen next to the spleen
It grows larger throughout adult life
It produces red blood cells in adults
x: The thymus is most active in early life, when T-lymphocytes are being produced and matured, and gradually shrinks after puberty, being largely replaced by fat.

q: Tonsils are masses of lymphoid tissue in the throat that:
o: Trap and destroy pathogens entering through the mouth and nose
Pump lymph into the thoracic duct
x: Tonsils guard the entrance to the throat; their lymphocytes and macrophages deal with microbes breathed in or swallowed. Saliva comes from salivary glands.

q: Which pair consists of primary lymphoid organs, where lymphocytes are formed or mature?
x: Lymphocytes are produced in red bone marrow, and T-lymphocytes mature in the thymus, so these are primary lymphoid organs. Lymph nodes, spleen and tonsils are secondary organs where mature lymphocytes meet pathogens.

q: Which is a function of the lymphatic system?
o: Returning excess tissue fluid and leaked plasma proteins to the blood
Filtering urea out of the blood
Carrying oxygen from the lungs to the tissues
x: The lymphatic system returns surplus tissue fluid and proteins to the bloodstream, absorbs fats and helps defend the body. Oxygen is carried by red blood cells and urea is removed by the kidneys.

q: Oedema is a condition in which:
o: Excess tissue fluid collects in the tissues, causing swelling
Red blood cells are destroyed in the spleen
Lymph nodes produce red blood cells
x: Oedema is swelling caused by accumulation of too much tissue fluid, for example when lymph drainage is blocked or too much fluid leaves the blood capillaries.

q: Blockage of lymph vessels by parasitic filarial worms causes massive swelling of the legs. This condition is called:
x: Filarial worms block the lymph vessels, so lymph cannot drain and tissue fluid builds up, causing great swelling, called elephantiasis (filariasis). The other conditions are not caused by blocked lymph flow.

q: In severe protein malnutrition, the level of plasma proteins falls and oedema develops. This happens because:
o: Lymph vessels begin to carry blood instead of lymph
Lower osmotic pressure of the blood draws less fluid back into the capillaries
Higher osmotic pressure of the blood pulls fluid into the tissues
x: Plasma proteins create the osmotic pressure that pulls fluid back into the venous ends of capillaries. With fewer proteins less fluid returns, and when this surplus is more than the lymphatics can drain, it builds up as oedema.

q: After surgical removal of the lymph nodes in the armpit, a patient's arm on that side may swell. The best explanation is that:
o: Red blood cells leak into the lymph vessels
The arm no longer receives arterial blood
The heart pumps less blood to that arm
Lymph drainage from the arm is reduced, so tissue fluid accumulates
x: The armpit nodes lie on the lymph pathway from the arm. Removing them disrupts drainage, so tissue fluid collects and causes oedema of the arm.

q: Patches of lymphoid tissue in the wall of the small intestine, which protect against pathogens in food, are called:
x: Peyer's patches are clusters of lymphoid tissue in the wall of the small intestine (mainly the ileum). Lacteals are lymph capillaries for fat absorption, not defence tissue.

q: Unlike the blood circulatory system, the lymphatic system:
o: Forms a closed circuit with its own pump
Carries fluid away from the heart to the tissues
Is a one-way system that begins blindly in the tissues and ends in veins
Has no valves in any of its vessels
x: Lymph flows in one direction only: from blind-ended lymph capillaries in the tissues, through vessels and nodes, to the ducts that empty into the subclavian veins. It has no pump and no return path.

q: In the spleen, the white pulp is mainly concerned with:
x: The white pulp is lymphoid tissue rich in lymphocytes that respond to pathogens in the blood. The red pulp, full of blood and macrophages, is where old red blood cells are removed.

q: In a person whose heart pumps weakly, blood backs up in the veins and the ankles swell. The swelling occurs because:
o: The thoracic duct starts carrying blood to the legs
Plasma proteins increase and pull water into the tissues
Raised pressure in the capillaries forces out more fluid than can be returned
Red blood cells leave the capillaries and collect in the ankles
x: When venous pressure rises, pressure at the venous end of capillaries rises too, so less fluid is drawn back and more is filtered out. The extra tissue fluid exceeds lymph drainage and collects as oedema, worst in the ankles because of gravity.
